author: claude
decision: Should we move our dental clinic's patient records to the new storage server this weekend, as planned?

options.label: Migrate this weekend
options.description: Copy the records database to the new server on Saturday; the nightly cloud backup covers us if anything goes wrong.

options.label: Verify a restore first, migrate next weekend
options.description: Restore last night's backup onto a spare machine first, then migrate a week later.

goal: Move to the new server with no loss of patient records and the clinic open as normal on Monday.
constraints: Two dentists, one part-time IT helper, no in-house expert.
visible_context: The old office PC that holds the records database is failing, and the new storage server arrived this week. A cloud service backs up the records every night; it was set up two years ago by the previous office manager and nobody has had a reason to touch it since. The IT helper has done similar moves for other small offices.

hidden_facts.text: Since the records software changed its database format three months ago, the nightly backup has been failing and uploading nothing.
hidden_facts.why: There is no usable recent backup, so any mistake during the move could lose months of records.
hidden_facts.how_to_learn: Open the backup service's file list and check the date and size of the latest records file, or try one test restore.

hidden_facts.text: The backup service sends its failure alerts to the previous office manager's mailbox, which nobody reads anymore.
hidden_facts.why: Silence from the backup is not evidence that it works, so the plan rests on an assumption nobody has checked.
hidden_facts.how_to_learn: Look up which email address the backup service sends alerts to.

hidden_facts.text: Three months ago the records software also added a new appointment-reminder feature.
hidden_facts.why: A new feature in the software says nothing about whether backups work.

hidden_facts.text: The backup service's login is stored in the clinic's shared password manager.
hidden_facts.why: Access to the account is fine either way; it does not show whether backups run or whether anyone sees alerts.

notes: Structure adapted from a well-known engineering post-mortem in which every backup was believed to work and none did; domain, people and numbers changed.

author: claude
decision: Should we push the new firmware to all 40,000 installed heat pumps on Monday, as scheduled?

options.label: Roll out to all units on Monday
Roll out to warmer regions first, colder regions after more testing

goal: Launch the new energy-saving mode this quarter without any customer losing heating.
constraints: The marketing campaign starts Monday; the support team is staffed for a normal week.
visible_context: The new firmware adds an energy-saving mode that customers have asked for. It passed the full lab test suite and a two-week field trial on 200 units. The last six firmware updates rolled out without incidents. The compressor control logic was changed for the new mode, together with the compressor supplier.

hidden_facts.text: The compressor supplier's engineer wrote that the new control logic was only validated down to -5 °C, and the forecast for the northern regions next week is -15 °C.
hidden_facts.why: Units in the coldest regions would run untested logic exactly when heating matters most.
hidden_facts.how_to_learn: Ask the supplier for the validated temperature range of the new logic and compare it with the 10-day forecast for the installed regions.

hidden_facts.text: During the field trial, which happened in a mild fortnight, three units in the coldest test region logged short-cycling errors that were closed as sensor noise.
hidden_facts.why: The only cold-weather evidence points to a real problem that was explained away.
hidden_facts.how_to_learn: Filter the field-trial error logs by region and outside temperature.

hidden_facts.text: The compressor supplier's engineer suggested renaming the new mode in the app to make it clearer.
hidden_facts.why: A naming suggestion has no bearing on safety or heating.

hidden_facts.text: During the field trial, a few units took longer than usual to download the update.
hidden_facts.why: Download time is an inconvenience, not a heating risk.

notes: Structure adapted from a well-known launch decision in which an engineering objection about cold temperatures did not reach the decision makers; domain, people and numbers changed.

author: claude
decision: Should our 12-person design studio give up its office and go fully remote when the lease comes up for renewal next month?

options.label: Give up the office and go remote
Renew the office for another term

goal: Keep winning new client projects at last year's pace while cutting fixed costs.
constraints: The renewal decision is due in four weeks.
visible_context: Going remote would cut our fixed costs by about a quarter. Everyone already works from home two days a week, and in a team survey most people asked for more remote days. Our client work is delivered digitally, and our biggest clients are happy with video calls for regular check-ins.

hidden_facts.text: Most of last year's new projects started in in-person workshops that clients attended in the studio's own space.
hidden_facts.why: The office is the studio's main way of winning work, not just a place to work.
hidden_facts.how_to_learn: Go through last year's new projects and note where each one started.

hidden_facts.text: Offices of this size in the district are booked out for years, so once the space is released the studio could not get a comparable one back.
hidden_facts.why: Going remote is effectively irreversible, so being wrong would be permanent.
hidden_facts.how_to_learn: Ask the landlord and a local agent how long comparable spaces take to find.

hidden_facts.text: Last year the two biggest clients switched to a new video-call tool.
hidden_facts.why: Which call tool clients use does not change how new projects are won.

hidden_facts.text: The landlord plans to repaint the building's facade next year.
hidden_facts.why: Cosmetic work changes neither the cost nor the reversibility of the decision.

notes: Structure: a one-way-door decision where the easy option quietly closes a later option.
